title: Reading and Steering Representations of Materials-Science Mechanisms in an Open-Weight Language Model
abstract: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here we show that materials science mechanism information in the open-weight google/gemma-4-E4B-it model has three experimentally separable forms: concepts are readable in individual hidden states, constitutive orientation is carried by controlled transformations between states, and selected internal representations causally control engineering answers. We combine matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark and causal interventions. In 50 held-out materials descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks, and target-free word sets from both readouts enabled blinded identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark produced mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that this apparent physical organization was equally explained by numerical comparison. We therefore compared otherwise identical prompts in which only the direction of the physical input was reversed, asking whether the resulting hidden-state movement followed the supplied constitutive law. These state transformations ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws, whereas lexical controls were near chance. Bidirectional interventions shifted answer probabilities toward or away from the physically appropriate outcome across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and answer formats. Physical relationships were therefore more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone.
summary: This paper investigates whether large language models encode actual physics from materials science, moving beyond simple pattern matching. By applying advanced interpretability tools like Jacobian lenses and causal interventions, the authors demonstrate that physical laws are best revealed not by looking at static states, but by observing how the model's internal state changes when a physical input direction is systematically reversed.
main_problem: The core problem is determining if a large language model genuinely encodes and utilizes underlying physical laws (mechanisms) from materials science, or if it merely correlates surface-level textual cues.
main_result: Physical relationships are found to be more visible in controlled state changes (e.g., reversing input direction) than in the absolute hidden states alone, suggesting a mechanistic encoding within the model's latent space.
method: The authors employ advanced interpretability techniques including Jacobian lenses, causal interventions (state patching), and testing directional invariance by reversing physical inputs to probe the model's internal state transformations.
model_or_system: The study uses an open-weight language model (google/gemma-4-E4B-it) trained on materials science descriptions. The 'system' being analyzed is the model's high-dimensional hidden state space, which is treated as a representation of physical knowledge.
key_observables: Concept ranks derived from readouts, directional law adherence (e.g., 39/40 correct reversals), and shifts in answer probabilities following causal interventions.
important_parameters: The analysis focuses on state transformations, the structure of constitutive laws, and the comparison between absolute states versus controlled changes in those states.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that physical mechanisms can be mapped onto mathematically measurable properties within the model's hidden state vectors, requiring careful disentanglement from mere lexical correlation.
figures_summary: Figures summarize evaluations using vocabulary readouts (concepts), matched counterfactual comparisons (state changes/constitutive orientation), and causal intervention tests (answer shifts).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing three separable forms of mechanism information: concepts in states, constitutive orientation via state transformations, and causal control over answers. It uses a multi-stage testing protocol involving readouts, relational geometry checks, and final directional/causal interventions.
why_interesting: While the domain is materials science AI, the methodology—interpreting complex physical laws (constitutive relations) as geometric constraints or directional invariances within a high-dimensional latent space—is highly relevant to understanding how quantum mechanical principles might be encoded in neural network representations.
